strengths: Introduces a novel, well-curated benchmark of 224 polyhedra spanning eight geometrically well-defined classes (Platonic, Archimedean, Catalan, Johnson, stellations, Kepler-Poinsot, compounds, uniform non-convex), providing unambiguous ground truth on symmetry, convexity, and complexity that is largely absent in existing large-scale 3D datasets like Objaverse or OmniObject3D.

Includes both synthetic (Mitsuba-rendered) and real-world (hand-constructed paper models photographed indoors/outdoors) images, enabling study of the synthetic-to-real generalization gap, which is a meaningful and underexplored axis.

Covers four complementary experimental paradigms (monocular 3D reconstruction, 3D symmetry detection via linear probing, mental rotation tests, and zero-shot VLM classification), offering a multi-faceted view of geometric reasoning rather than a single narrow task.

Evaluates a reasonably broad and current set of models, including three monocular reconstruction methods, nine vision featurizers of different training paradigms, and four frontier VLMs (Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Gemini 2.5 Pro, ChatGPT o3/o4-mini-high).

Provides interesting and somewhat surprising findings, e.g., DINOv2 embeddings implicitly encode certain 3D symmetries well via linear probing yet all models struggle badly at discriminating geometrically similar shapes (near chance in synthetic-to-wild transfer), and frontier VLMs make systematic, interpretable errors regarding face geometry, convexity, and compound structure recognition.
Rich qualitative failure analysis of VLM reasoning traces adds interpretability value beyond raw accuracy numbers.
weaknesses: The monocular 3D reconstruction evaluation is very limited in scale (only three representative shapes shown qualitatively in a table), with no quantitative 3D metrics (e.g., Chamfer distance, IoU, F-score) despite claiming a 'systematic' evaluation; conclusions about reconstruction failures are drawn from a handful of qualitative examples.

The zero-shot VLM classification uses a single minimal prompt ('What is the name of this polyhedron?') with no exploration of prompting strategies (e.g., chain-of-thought, multi-turn, providing candidate answer lists), which may understate or bias the reported capabilities of the models.

No human baseline is reported for any of the four tasks, which would strengthen the benchmark's claims about specific gaps between model and human geometric reasoning (motivated heavily by cognitive science framing in the intro/related work).

The symmetry detection task is restricted to only three symmetry types (central point reflection, 4-fold and 5-fold rotation), which is a fairly narrow slice of the rich symmetry taxonomy the paper itself describes (e.g., no edge/face-transitivity probes, no reflective symmetry planes beyond these).

Several details are deferred to supplementary material that seem central to interpreting the main claims (e.g., full MRT results, dataset splits, per-featurizer combination method comparisons), making the main text evaluation feel less self-contained and harder to fully assess from the paper alone.

The contribution is primarily a curated benchmark/dataset rather than a new method or theoretical insight; while valuable, this places a high bar on breadth/depth of evaluation that is only partially met given the small-scale reconstruction study and single-prompt VLM evaluation.

Minor writing issues, e.g., an apparently redacted/missing attribution ('constructed by .') in Section 3.4, and the dataset link itself is not shown, raising minor concerns about completeness/reproducibility at this stage.

strengths: The dataset itself is a genuinely novel resource: 224 polyhedra spanning Platonic, Archimedean, Catalan, Johnson, stellation, Kepler-Poinsot, compound, and uniform non-convex classes, with both physically-rendered synthetic images and real paper-model photographs under varied indoor/outdoor conditions — this breadth of fine-grained, mathematically well-defined 3D shapes is uncommon in existing 3D vision benchmarks.

The four complementary evaluation paradigms (monocular reconstruction, symmetry linear-probing, mental rotation test, zero-shot VLM classification) target genuinely distinct aspects of geometric reasoning and together paint a coherent picture of model limitations.

The qualitative failure-case analysis of frontier VLMs (Claude, Gemini, GPT-o3/o4) is illustrative and provides some insight into specific reasoning errors (face-type misidentification, convexity confusion, compound misclassification).

The linear-probing experiment on symmetry detection is methodologically reasonable (weighted BCE for imbalance, balanced accuracy, train/test split by held-out shapes) and produces an interesting, specific finding (DINOv2 outperforms other featurizers on 4-fold rotational symmetry).
weaknesses: The monocular reconstruction evaluation is almost entirely qualitative: only three representative shapes (cube, great dodecahedron, small cubicuboctahedron) are shown with visual renderings in a table, with no quantitative metrics (Chamfer distance, IoU, F-score, normal consistency) reported across the 224-shape dataset despite the dataset's scale being advertised as a core contribution. This severely undercuts the claimed 'systematic' evaluation.

Sample sizes for several experiments appear very small and are not clearly reported: it is unclear how many images per category were used in the zero-shot VLM classification experiment, whether results are averaged over multiple viewpoints, and what the variance/confidence intervals are. Figure 3a accuracy values per category look like they could be based on only a handful of examples per class.

The 'hard split' construction for the Mental Rotation Test relies on manual, subjective selection of 'visually similar' pairs (Table 4), which is not rigorously defined or validated (e.g., no inter-rater agreement, no systematic similarity metric), raising reproducibility and bias concerns.

The paper's own categorization of polyhedra groups is stated to be 'arbitrary' (Table 1 caption), which weakens the rigor of using these categories as the basis for quantitative breakdowns of model performance throughout the experiments.

Key dataset construction details are redacted/missing in the text (e.g., 'constructed by _______' in Sec 3.4), and there is insufficient detail on camera calibration, pose annotation for real images, or how ground-truth 3D geometry/symmetry labels were obtained and verified for the real photographs, raising reproducibility concerns.

The paper tests only a small, fixed set of proprietary frontier VLMs (4 models) and provides no statistical testing or multiple-trial averaging, and the single-prompt zero-shot protocol ('What is the name of this polyhedron?') may not reflect the models' actual geometric reasoning capability under more informative prompting.

No new method or algorithmic contribution is proposed to address the identified gaps; the paper is purely diagnostic, which is acceptable for a benchmark paper but the shallow quantitative analysis in the reconstruction task in particular makes the diagnostic value limited.

Related work and framing emphasize the dataset's uniqueness, but there is limited quantitative comparison (e.g., table of dataset statistics vs. OmniObject3D/ShapeNet/Objaverse in terms of annotation richness) that would substantiate the significance claim beyond prose assertions.

The writing in places overclaims rigor and comprehensiveness ('systematic experiments', 'comprehensive collection') that is not matched by the actual experimental depth, particularly in Section 4.1 where only 3 shapes and qualitative visualization are used.

strengths: Introduces a novel and carefully curated benchmark of 224 polyhedra spanning Platonic, Archimedean, Catalan, Johnson, stellations, Kepler-Poinsot, compound, and uniform non-convex classes, providing unambiguous, well-defined geometric ground truth (symmetry group, convexity, face type) that is missing from existing large-scale 3D datasets like Objaverse or OmniObject3D.

Includes both synthetic renderings (Mitsuba) and painstakingly hand-constructed real paper polyhedra photographed in diverse indoor/outdoor conditions, giving a valuable sim-to-real generalization axis that is rare in this kind of geometric benchmark.

Evaluates a wide and relevant set of models/tasks: monocular 3D reconstruction (Shap-E, SF3D, OpenLRM), linear-probe symmetry detection across 9 featurizers, mental rotation tests, and zero-shot classification with 4 frontier VLMs (Claude, Gemini, GPT-o3/o4-mini), giving a fairly comprehensive picture of current model limitations.

The qualitative failure analysis of VLM reasoning (Table 3b) is insightful and clearly illustrates systematic errors (face-type hallucination, convexity confusion, compound misidentification), which is useful for the community beyond raw accuracy numbers.
The paper is well-written, historically motivated, and the geometric preliminaries are clearly presented, making the benchmark accessible even to non-specialists in polyhedral geometry.
weaknesses: The monocular 3D reconstruction evaluation (Sec 4.1) is very limited in scale (only 3 representative shapes) and purely qualitative (visual renderings in a table), with no quantitative metrics such as Chamfer distance, IoU, or F-score, undermining the strength of the claimed findings.

There is an unexplained discrepancy between the stated total of 224 polyhedra and the sum of category counts in Table 1 (5+13+13+92+48+4+10+53 = 238), suggesting overlapping categories (e.g., Kepler-Poinsot as a subset of stellations) that are not clearly explained.

No human baseline is reported for the mental rotation test or symmetry detection tasks, despite MRT being originally a well-established human psychometric test; without this anchor, it is hard to gauge how large the model-human gap actually is.

The 'hard' MRT pairs and some categorizations (e.g., Table 1 grouping) are described as manually/arbitrarily selected, raising concerns about selection bias and reproducibility of these specific splits.

Zero-shot VLM classification is based on a single fixed prompt with no prompt-engineering or chain-of-thought variants explored, and only 4 (or a handful of) models are tested without statistical significance analysis or multiple trials to account for VLM output variance.

The real 'wild' paper models, while impressive in engineering effort, are a specific proxy for real-world objects (thin, foldable material with visible seams) that may not fully represent the distribution shift challenges of true real-world rigid 3D objects.
Some result tables/figures (e.g., Fig. 2, Fig. 3a) lack error bars or confidence intervals, limiting interpretability of small differences between models.

Anonymized details (dataset link, physical model creator) are redacted in the current version, which is expected for review but leaves some reproducibility aspects (exact download/access process) currently unverifiable.

strengths: Introduces a novel, well-curated benchmark (GIQ) spanning a wide taxonomy of polyhedra (Platonic, Archimedean, Catalan, Johnson, Kepler-Poinsot, stellations, compounds) with mathematically precise ground-truth properties, addressing a real gap in existing 3D benchmarks like Objaverse that lack fine-grained symmetry/geometry annotations.

Substantial data collection effort: 224 unique shapes rendered synthetically plus physically constructed paper models photographed under varied indoor/outdoor real-world conditions, providing a useful sim-to-real testbed.

Comprehensive multi-task evaluation covering four complementary facets of geometric reasoning (monocular reconstruction, symmetry probing, mental rotation, zero-shot VLM classification), touching diverse model families (reconstruction models, self-/supervised encoders, multi-view geometry networks, frontier VLMs, geometry-native 3D LLMs).

Inclusion of a human baseline user study for the mental rotation task strengthens the claims by contextualizing model performance against human performance rather than relying on accuracy numbers alone.

Findings are interesting and diagnostic: strong linear probe performance for symmetry detection contrasts with poor performance on fine-grained mental rotation and VLM shape classification, illustrating a nuanced picture of implicit vs. explicit geometric understanding.
Qualitative error analysis of VLM failures (confusing convexity, conflating compounds/stellations, hallucinating faces) adds interpretability beyond aggregate accuracy numbers.
weaknesses: Much of the quantitative evidence is deferred to the appendix (e.g., reconstruction is only shown qualitatively for 3 shapes in the main text with no numerical metrics like Chamfer distance or IoU), weakening the self-contained rigor of the main paper.
The reconstruction evaluation is limited to only three representative shapes, which is a small and possibly non-representative sample for concluding broad failure across complexity levels.

The paper is primarily an evaluation/benchmark study using existing off-the-shelf methods (linear/non-linear probes, pretrained reconstruction and VLM models) without proposing new techniques or remedies, limiting technical novelty despite the useful diagnostic contribution.
Some categorization choices are acknowledged as arbitrary by the authors themselves (overlapping counts, e.g., 238 vs 224), which could affect reproducibility/clarity of exact task splits.

Sample sizes per polyhedron category for zero-shot VLM classification are not clearly reported in the main text, making it hard to assess the statistical reliability of category-wise accuracy differences.

No experiments explore whether fine-tuning or targeted training (rather than just probing/zero-shot evaluation) could close the observed geometric reasoning gaps, limiting the paper's actionable insights beyond diagnosis.
The redacted phrase regarding who constructed the physical models suggests some incomplete anonymization/preparation of the manuscript.

Only a single fixed prompt is used for the primary VLM classification, and while CoT/multi-view ablations are attempted, the exploration of prompting strategies remains fairly limited given known prompt-sensitivity of VLMs.

strengths: Introduces a carefully curated, mathematically well-defined benchmark of 224 polyhedra spanning Platonic, Archimedean, Catalan, Johnson, Kepler-Poinsot, stellations, and compound solids, with both synthetic renders and physically constructed real-world images.
Covers four complementary evaluation axes (monocular reconstruction, symmetry probing, mental rotation, zero-shot classification), giving a reasonably broad picture of geometric reasoning gaps.
Includes a human baseline user study for the mental rotation task, which is a nice addition often missing from similar benchmark papers.
Evaluates a wide range of models/encoders (CLIP, DINO/DINOv2, SigLIP, MAE, ConvNext, VGGT, DUSt3R, MASt3R) as well as frontier VLMs and 3D-native LLMs, providing a broad comparison.

The use of well-defined polyhedral symmetry groups provides unambiguous ground truth, which is a reasonable design choice for isolating geometric properties from confounds present in generic 3D object datasets.
weaknesses: Quantitative rigor for the reconstruction task is weak: the main text (Table 1) only shows qualitative renderings for three example shapes with no numerical metrics (e.g., Chamfer distance, F-score, normal consistency) presented in the main paper, undermining the central claim that reconstruction 'fails' in a measurable sense.

The reconstruction baselines (Shap-E, SF3D, OpenLRM) are relatively dated; more recent, stronger single-image-to-3D methods (e.g., more recent diffusion/Gaussian-based reconstruction models) are omitted, weakening claims about the state of the art.

The dataset itself is small (224 shapes), and several experiments further reduce coverage (e.g., excluding Johnson solids from the symmetry task 'due to ambiguities'), which raises concerns about statistical robustness of the 5-fold cross-validation and generalizability of conclusions.

The polyhedral categorization is explicitly acknowledged by the authors as 'arbitrary', and several other methodological choices (hard-split construction criteria for MRT, symmetry class definitions) are not fully specified in the main text, reducing reproducibility and rigor.

The core findings largely reconfirm results already established in prior literature (VLMs lack 3D/depth awareness, reconstruction models struggle out-of-distribution, mental rotation is hard for models) without introducing new methods or mitigation strategies, limiting the paper's novelty and impact beyond being an additional diagnostic dataset.

No new method, training strategy, or model improvement is proposed; the paper is purely diagnostic/benchmark-focused, and the promised future directions (e.g., CoT training data generation) are speculative and not demonstrated.
The anonymized placeholder ('constructed by ___') suggests parts of the manuscript were not fully proofread/prepared for review, raising minor concerns about overall polish.

Human study sample size (42 participants) and lack of statistical significance testing across many model comparisons (e.g., differences between DINOv2, SigLIP, and other encoders) leave some conclusions under-supported by rigorous statistical analysis.

strengths: Introduces a novel, well-curated benchmark (GIQ) spanning 224 unique polyhedra across mathematically well-defined categories (Platonic, Archimedean, Catalan, Johnson, stellations, compounds, Kepler-Poinsot, uniform non-convex), providing unambiguous ground truth for symmetry, convexity, and complexity that prior large-scale 3D datasets (Objaverse, OmniObject3D) lack.

Combines synthetic (Mitsuba-rendered) and real-world (physically constructed paper models photographed indoors/outdoors) imagery, enabling cross-domain generalization analysis that is rare in this line of work.

Comprehensive, multi-faceted evaluation protocol covering four distinct but complementary tasks (monocular reconstruction, 3D symmetry probing, mental rotation, zero-shot classification), giving a broad picture of geometric reasoning gaps rather than a single narrow metric.

Tests a wide and current range of models: reconstruction methods (Shap-E, SF3D, OpenLRM), 12 image encoders spanning supervised/self-supervised/geometry-native architectures, and four frontier VLMs plus 3D-aware LLMs (LLaVA-3D, ShapeLLM, PointLLM/PointBind), giving good coverage of the current model landscape.

Includes a genuine human-subject baseline (42 participants) for the mental rotation task, offering a meaningful point of comparison against models and strengthening the claims about the human-model gap.

Uses sound experimental practices such as 5-fold cross-validation with shape-level splits for probing, weighted loss for class imbalance, and both linear/non-linear probes to check for encoding robustness.
Qualitative failure analysis (confusing convexity, conflating compounds and stellations, hallucinated face types) is illustrative and adds interpretability to the quantitative results.
weaknesses: The main text lacks quantitative reconstruction metrics (e.g., Chamfer distance, IoU) for the monocular 3D reconstruction task; only qualitative renderings for three representative shapes are shown in Table 1, making it hard to judge the magnitude of failure or compare methods rigorously without consulting the appendix.

Several important experimental details (hard-split construction criteria for MRT, full quantitative results by domain, non-linear probe comparisons, ablations on CoT/multi-view prompting) are deferred entirely to the appendix, leaving the main text somewhat incomplete for independent assessment.

Placeholder blanks remain in the text (e.g., dataset URL in the abstract, and 'constructed by ___' in Section 3.4), suggesting incomplete anonymization/editing that could indicate the manuscript was not fully proofread before submission.

Real-world ('wild') coverage is uneven across categories—for instance, only 48 of 92 Johnson solids have real photographs—which could bias cross-domain comparisons for the hardest, most fine-grained category.

The synthetic renderings use a fixed yellowish material while real models are multi-colored; this stylistic mismatch between domains is a potential confound for the reported cross-domain (synthetic-to-wild) generalization results that is not discussed or controlled for.

The paper is purely diagnostic; no experiments explore whether fine-tuning or targeted training on GIQ-like data can close the identified gaps, limiting insight into actionable remedies beyond general statements in the conclusion.

Some concluding claims (e.g., framing GIQ as a prerequisite for 'geometric calculus' of complex scenes, or relevance to 'rigid and fluid dynamics') are speculative and not directly supported by the experiments presented.

The relationship between the implicit (linear-probe) symmetry detection results and the explicit reasoning failures (MRT, VLM classification) is asserted but not deeply analyzed—e.g., no correlation analysis linking probe accuracy to downstream reasoning failure to substantiate the 'implicit vs explicit' narrative.
